name: Uma Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I milk 65 cows on the farm my grandfather started, about 80 hectares of grass, maize and a bit of barley up the Halden valley. Milking is at half five and again at four, and in between it's feeding, scraping the yards, fieldwork and whatever's broken. My husband Per drives the school bus part-time and helps with the evening milking. We've a mortgage from when we bought my brother out of his half of the farm six years ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a good day, and what's a bad one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good day is when the milk tanker comes on time, the cows are all on their feet and I get the silage in before the rain. A bad day is a cow with mastitis, a vet bill and the milk price letter from Northvale Dairies all in the same week. I don't use computers much, Per does the online forms for the dairy. I'd rather be in the parlour than looking at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and leave it at that. People get excited about every new thing, and most of it turns out to be a better kettle. At the market I'd say what I always say: watch the milk price, not the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changing on the farm isn't the same as nothing to worry about. The milk price has dropped twice in two years, and every time it does, we're a month closer to empty. The mortgage on my brother's half still has fourteen years to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on milking twice a day exactly as we do. I'd put off replacing the old feed wagon for another year and patch it up instead, which saves about 20,000 we don't have anyway. And I'd ask Per to look at cheaper electricity for the parlour, because that bill has nearly doubled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Same worries, just no new ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the milk price drops again next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut back at home first: no holiday, the kids' clubs cut down to one each. If it went on more than six months, I'd sell ten of the older cows to pay the feed bill. I've watched my dad do that in the nineties, and it nearly broke him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Per's bus job help much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It covers the food shop and the kids' school things, more or less. It's not a lot of money, but it's money that comes in when the milk price doesn't. Without it, we'd have been in real trouble two winters ago.

say: Most new things turn out to be **a better kettle**.
I'd tell people at the market to **watch the milk price**, not the news.
think: Nothing changes, but **nothing changing** isn't the same as nothing to worry about.
Each **milk price drop** brings us a month closer to empty.
do: Patch up the **old feed wagon** for another year instead of replacing it.
Get Per to find **cheaper electricity** for the milking parlour.
Keep milking **twice a day** exactly as now.
feel: **Tired**, with the same old worries and no new ones.
S0.quote: Nothing changing on the farm isn't the same as nothing to worry about.
fieldNote: Uma's worries are **milk price and mortgage**, long before AI enters it.
She's **plain-spoken** and distrusts excitement about anything new.
Per's **bus wage** is the household's quiet safety net.
She'd **cut back** before changing how she farms.

steps.text: Keep milking the 65 cows twice a day as now
Patch the old feed wagon instead of spending 20,000 on a new one
Have Per switch the parlour to a cheaper electricity deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's problem more than mine. Northvale Dairies would probably move all its forms and its phone line to AI, and I'd moan about not getting a real person. Nobody's milking cows with a chatbot, so the office people at Northvale Dairies can worry about this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't feel like it's coming for me yet. Half the neighbours already have robot milkers, and I've said no for ten years because they cost 150,000 and break down at night. If the robots spread slowly, I'll be the last one in the valley still milking by hand, and I'm fine with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking the same way. Per would deal with the dairy's new online system, because he's the one who does the forms already. I'd wait a couple of years and see how the neighbours get on before I even think about any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Everyone around me changing and me standing still, that's an odd feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said half the neighbours have robot milkers. What do you see when you visit them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I see Jens next door checking his phone at dinner because the robot's sent him an alarm. His cows are fine, and his milk yield went up, I won't lie. But he's paying the loan for twelve years and he's never really off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the dairy paid more for robot milk, or paid less for mine, I'd have to think about it. Or if my back went, which it might, the way it's been this winter. But I'd want to see five years of a neighbour's robot working before I signed anything.

say: The change hits **office people** like Northvale's staff more than farmers.
Nobody's **milking cows** with a chatbot, whatever the dairy does with its phones.
think: The change doesn't feel like it's **coming for me** yet.
I've refused **robot milkers** for ten years because of cost and breakdowns.
do: Leave the dairy's **new online system** to Per, who does the forms already.
**Wait two years** and watch the neighbours before considering any change.
Keep **milking by hand** in the old parlour.
feel: **Uneasy**, standing still while everyone around me changes.
S1.quote: Nobody's milking cows with a chatbot, so the office people at Northvale Dairies can worry about this one.
fieldNote: Uma is **sure of her ground**: dairy work stays hands-on in this picture.
She's watched **neighbours' robots** closely and has fair reasons to hold back.
A **bad back** or a price change at the dairy could force her hand.
She **relies on Per** for anything on a screen.

steps.text: Keep milking by hand in the old parlour
Watch neighbours' robot milkers for two years before deciding anything
Hand the dairy's new online system to Per

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast for anyone to cope with, and someone should slow it down. I'm not one for protests, but I'd sign anything the farmers' union put round. At the market I'd say the small dairies are done for if nobody steps in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it finishes us as a dairy. By 2031 the big robot dairies are making milk cheaper than we can, and Northvale will take their milk first and drop small suppliers. I'm 43, I've only ever milked cows, and we still owe fourteen years on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the honest answer. I'd stop every bit of spending that isn't feed or the mortgage, so no new wagon, no holiday, nothing. I'd try to put another 400 a month aside from the milk cheque while the price lasts. And I'd go and see the farm advisory service about what help there is for dairies, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd lie awake doing sums that don't come out for a 65-cow dairy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The dairy's office work changes in 2028, and the robots come around 2031. What happens in between?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In between I'd still be milking, but I'd be watching the dairy's new contracts like a hawk. They'd use their AI to work out which farms are worth collecting from, and I bet a 65-cow farm on a hill road loses. Those three years would just be waiting for the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd wait and see in other pictures. Would you wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I couldn't afford to. Waiting is fine when there's time, but two years isn't time. I'd hate it, but I'd have to think about selling the herd while cows are still worth something.

say: This is going **too fast**, and someone should slow it down.
The **small dairies** are done for unless someone steps in.
think: I expect **robot dairies** to undercut us and Northvale to drop small suppliers.
I've **only milked cows** and still owe fourteen years on the mortgage.
do: Stop every bit of spending except **feed and mortgage**.
Save an **extra 400 a month** from the milk cheque while prices last.
Visit the **farm advisory service** about help for dairies, for the first time.
feel: **Scared**, lying awake doing sums that don't come out.
S2.quote: I'd lie awake doing sums that don't come out for a 65-cow dairy.
fieldNote: Uma expects to **lose the dairy income** and admits she has no clear plan.
For once she **can't wait**, and even considers selling the herd.
She sees the three-year gap as **waiting for a letter** from the dairy.
Asking for **outside help** is new for her, and she says so.

steps.text: Stop all spending except feed and the mortgage
Save an extra 400 a month from the milk cheque
Visit the farm advisory service about help for small dairies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same mess, just with a few more years to get ready. I'd tell people there's no point panicking yet, but no point pretending either. At the farmers' union meeting I'd ask what the plan is for small dairies, because someone should have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd still lose the dairy, just around 2034 instead of 2031. By then Freya would be 23 and Ole 19, so the kids would be off our hands, mostly. That's a big difference to me, the kids being through school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait the first couple of years to see if it's really coming, because I've seen plenty of things that didn't. I'd keep saving whatever the milk cheque allows, aiming for six months put by. And I'd sit down with Ole, who loves the cows, and tell him not to plan his life around taking on the dairy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It's not on top of me like the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ole, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, keep helping with the calves, but learn a trade that isn't cows. Maybe mechanics, like my brother. Telling my son Ole that would hurt, because I always pictured him in the parlour after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the dairy did go in 2034, what would you do with the land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably rent the grass to a bigger farm and keep the house. I'd find some work, maybe on someone else's farm doing what the robots can't, or helping Per with the buses. I haven't thought about it properly, I'll be honest.

say: It's the **same mess**, with a few more years to get ready.
There's no point **panicking yet**, but no point pretending either.
think: I'd still **lose the dairy**, just around 2034 instead of 2031.
By then the **kids are through school**, which matters hugely to me.
do: **Wait two years** to see whether it's really coming.
Save from the **milk cheque** toward six months put by.
Tell Ole not to plan his life around **taking on the dairy**.
S3.quote: Telling my son Ole that would hurt, because I always pictured him in the parlour after me.
fieldNote: Uma's plan hinges on the **kids finishing school** before the robots come.
Her biggest move is telling **her son** to learn another trade.
She falls back on **wait and see**, her usual habit, for the first years.
She hasn't thought through **life after the dairy** and says so.

steps.text: Wait two years to see whether the change is real
Save from the milk cheque toward six months of cushion
Tell Ole to learn a trade other than dairy farming

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time in farming, and a lot can change. I'd tell people not to sell up in a hurry. Plenty of things everyone said would happen never did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd milk until about 2039 and then stop. I'd be 56, the mortgage would have four years left, and the kids would be grown. It's not the life I planned, but it's one I could live with, if the milk price holds until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do nothing different, honestly. I'd keep milking, keep the old parlour going and keep the money tight like always. I'd start a savings pot for Freya and Ole's training, so whatever they do, they're not stuck like I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Still a knot in my stomach, but a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if the milk price holds. What if it doesn't, in the years before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's the same as now: cut back, sell some older cows, and hope. That's what I'd be doing anyway, AI or not. The robots just put an end date on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the long warning tempt you to buy a robot milker after all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Paying off a 150,000 robot milker over twelve years when the end is coming in thirteen doesn't make sense to me. Jens would say I'm stubborn, and he'd be right, but the sums are on my side this time.

say: Ten years is a **long time** in farming, and a lot can change.
People shouldn't **sell up** in a hurry, because plenty of predictions never happen.
think: I'd milk until about **2039** and stop at 56.
It isn't the life I planned, but I **could live with** it if milk prices hold.
do: Change **nothing** in the first year and keep money tight.
Start a **savings pot** for Freya's and Ole's training.
Keep the **old parlour** running instead of buying a robot milker.
feel: **Better**, with a smaller knot in my stomach.
S4.quote: Paying off a 150,000 robot milker over twelve years when the end is coming in thirteen doesn't make sense to me.
fieldNote: Uma plans to **milk until 2039** and stop, with the kids grown by then.
Her ongoing fear is the **milk price**, which the decade doesn't fix.
She **refuses robots** on cost grounds and admits she's stubborn.
Her one change is a **training fund** for her children.

steps.text: Keep milking in the old parlour without buying a robot
Start a savings pot for Freya's and Ole's training
Keep household spending tight to hold the cushion

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have two kids at school and no plan. What would actually help is the dairy promising to keep collecting from small farms for a set number of years, so we could plan. And some proper help from the advisory service about what else we could do with the land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everybody talks about jobs, but the cows have names in our shed. Whatever happens, I'd want them going to someone who'll look after them properly.

headlineQuote: Everybody talks about jobs, but the cows have names in our shed.
portrait: Uma Jensen is a 43-year-old **dairy farmer** milking 65 cows on her grandfather's farm.
She **avoids new technology**, leaves screens to her husband Per and has refused robot milkers.
Her steady worry is the **milk price** and a mortgage from buying out her brother.
Fast AGI frightens her most because she has **no plan** and two kids at school.
With more warning she plans to **milk until 2039** and steer her son elsewhere.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with two kids at school and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **dairy promise** to keep collecting from small farms for set years.
**Advisory help** on what else to do with the land.
